title: Drone Strikes Are Destroying the Infrastructure of Survival in the Heart of Sudan

_Story by_ _Mohamed Wad Al-Sak_

Ahmed Mahmoud's sister, Nafisah, died last month in the city of El-Obeid,
another victim of a more than three-year long war raging across Sudan already
considered one of the deadliest conflicts for civilians this century.

But like a growing number of Sudanese victims of the war, Mahmoud's sister's
death was not the direct result of an airstrike, or gunfire. Instead, she fell
victim to the near-total collapse of basic infrastructure in the country as a
result of calculated attacks aimed at depriving Sudanese civilians the
necessities of life.

The war in Sudan has now killed somewhere between 150,000 to 400,000 people
[according](https://www.csis.org/analysis/sudan-war-10-charts) to outside
analysts, with people dying from a combination of direct violence, hunger, and
lack of access to healthcare.

In June, the 21-year-old Nafisah suddenly fell faint and needed urgent
hospital care; she had been managing the impact of an under-treated blood clot
in her left leg since 2024. With El-Obeid under constant drone attack and
bombardment conducted by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF),
receiving prompt medical care for basic conditions was nearly impossible.

"We called the ambulance and waited a long time for any tuk-tuk or private
car. Then we were told that movement was difficult because of the conditions
and the fuel shortage," Mahmoud said. Blood clots can be life-threatening
without immediate medical treatment. "After that we started looking for any
car or way to move her. But time kept passing, and her condition kept getting
worse."

When they finally did reach the hospital, the facility was facing resource and
personnel strains due to the war and overwhelmed with patients. "When we
arrived we found the doctors trying to help everyone, but the pressure was
immense and resources were limited. It was clear they were working under
extremely difficult conditions," he said.

His sister died several hours after arriving at the hospital. Her death still
haunts her family members, who believe that the delay in arriving at the
facility and receiving treatment contributed to her death.

"After she died, I kept thinking: if the ambulance had arrived faster, or if
the services hadn't broken down, maybe my sister would still be with us,"
Mahmoud said. "People think war only kills those struck by shells. But the
truth is it also kills when it prevents a patient from reaching treatment. My
sister was one of them."

## **War on Infrastructure**

The crisis that has overtaken hospitals and other infrastructure in El-Obeid
is the product of a calculated military campaign waged by the RSF that has
directly targeted civilian infrastructure and imposed a de facto siege.

In recent months, the RSF, which receives arms and other support from the
United Arab Emirates, has begun using bombardment by foreign-supplied drones
to destroy critical infrastructure, attack supply lines, and force the
capitulation of the city's population.

El-Obeid itself remains under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).
Its 5th Infantry Division is headquartered in the city, which serves as the
army's main operational base in North Kordofan, after being pushed out of the
Sudanese capital of Khartoum, and falling back toward its western strongholds
in Darfur last year, the group no longer has the manpower or heavy equipment
to mount a direct ground assault and seize the city outright.

Lacking the ability to launch a direct assault, the RSF has reverted to
besieging the entire city--cutting supply lines into El-Obeid and striking
infrastructure with drones on a regular basis. El-Obeid has experienced a
spike in aerial attacks since mid-June, according to the [global monitor group
Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED](https://acleddata.com/media-
citation/fears-massacre-city-front-line-sudans-war-bbc)).

Those findings are echoed by local residents who say that drone attacks by the
RSF have intensified against the city, targeting fuel and water infrastructure
while making many roadways too dangerous to cross. For [five consecutive
days](https://sudantribune.com/article/315064#google_vignette) in the middle
of this month, strikes hit fuel stations in El-Obeid. On June 19, a
[strike](https://sudantribune.com/article/315248) on the main power
transformer cut off electricity entirely.

The price of food and fuel is skyrocketing as supplies disappear, while
families have resorted to digging wells in a desperate attempt to access water
of dubious safety. Nour al-Din Hajj al-Lain, 37, a transport worker in El-
Obeid, said that in the wake of the fuel station attacks, fuel prices have
reached approximately $30 per gallon with passenger fares rising by up to
2,000 pounds. "Many people are now walking to work," he said. "El-Obeid is a
principal transit point--when transport here is disrupted, the impact extends
across a wide area well beyond the city itself."

Adam Hamid, who has been working in El-Obeid's main market for about 15 years,
said most residents continue their daily lives despite mounting anxiety, but
that uncertainty and insecurity has already altered economic behavior. Before
the drone attacks made daily life in the city unsafe, the market was much
busier, Hamid said. His small shop, which sells household basics, used to
receive around 50-70 customers a day. That average has dropped to less than
half--dipping further on days following attacks, or when there are reports of
possible new strikes.

"Most customers now focus only on essential goods such as food and basic
necessities, while postponing non-essential purchases or larger expenses," he
explained. Traders are similarly cautious and have stopped buying large
quantities of goods or are reducing their operations. On June 24 members of
Congress [urged](https://democrats-foreignaffairs.house.gov/2026/6/meeks-
jacobs-issue-statement-on-rsf-siege-of-el-obeid) the State Department to
secure an agreement to lift the siege, which it said the RSF and its allies
have used to "collectively punish civilians and maximize death and
destruction."

## **Healthcare Disruptions**

Emergency first responders in El-Obeid today describe a nightmarish situation
in which shortages of fuel have left them unable to reach civilians in
distress, while drone attacks on major roads make it treacherous for
ambulances to travel even when fuel is available.

"Before, we used to move the moment we got a call. Now the first question we
ask is: is the road safe?" said an ambulance driver at a health facility in
the city, who asked not to be named for security reasons. "Often we delay or
take longer routes to avoid areas that might be targeted [by airstrikes],
which means the patient waits longer before help arrives."

For patients with hemorrhaging or blood clots--like the sister of Ahmed
Mahmoud--that delay can mean the difference between life and death.

Abdelmajeed Mohammed, a neurosurgeon in El-Obeid, said that the escalation of
attacks has transformed how the city's referral hospitals operate. "In a
single minute, 50 patients can come in, and life practically stops with the
shelling," said Mohammed.

Drone strikes, he added, have paralyzed every step of the medical system.

"Ambulances struggle to move because of fuel shortages and security risks,
medical staff are delayed getting to the hospital, and medical supplies are
disrupted," he said. "And if the power goes out or the generator fuel runs
dry, vital equipment--monitors, oxygen, operating rooms, dialysis machines--
all stop. That's why we say life inside the hospital nearly comes to a halt."

The strikes on fuel stations have also further crippled hospitals, which rely
on them to operate generators amid nationwide blackouts and strikes on
electrical power stations.

"Two days ago we were forced to suspend some emergency admissions because of a
power outage, and before that, surgeries were postponed because generator fuel
wasn't available," he said. "Fuel is the lifeline of the hospital for us.
Patients who need oxygen depend on machines that don't work without
electricity, and even the machines that read vital signs don't work without
electricity and fuel. And if you can't see the vital signs, you can't treat
the patient."

El-Obeid's Al-Jameeh Dialysis Center is one of the last medical centers
offering kidney dialysis in western Sudan after war shut down services across
the area. But now, it too is teetering.

Ayman Abdulrahman, one of the center's medical staff, said machines are
breaking down at a rapid clip because of the relentless flow of patients. At
the moment, all they can do is scale back services. "In the past we used to
give the patient two full sessions, but with the pressure and the machine
shortage we were forced to cut the session length so we could give other
patients a chance too."

A similar wave of strikes [in June
2023](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2023/6/15/%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%B6%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%84%D9%89-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%AF%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%B3%D8%A9-%D9%84%D9%84%D9%85%D9%88%D8%AA)
wreaked havoc on the dialysis unit, with at least 12 patients dying as a
result. So far there are no officially documented figures on how many deaths
have resulted at the center from the latest strikes.

"The work day now starts with the question: do we have electricity? Is there
enough fuel to run the generator?" said Esraa Awad, a doctor at the dialysis
center and its former director. "A patient hooked up to a dialysis machine
can't simply have their session stopped because of shelling or a power cut.
Any sudden interruption puts us in front of real medical risks."

Awad explained the fuel crisis extends beyond generators to patient transport
and the arrival of staff and supplies: "Dialysis isn't just a machine, it's an
interconnected chain. If the fuel or electricity is cut, or a patient or
supplies can't get through, the whole link collapses--and the patient is the
first to pay the price."

After the RSF stepped up its strikes on fuel-stations in June, it cut even
deeper into critical energy supplies for the city's hospitals, said an
emergency room nurse at Al-Daman Hospital, who asked not to be named for her
personal safety. "We now start every shift not knowing whether the power will
hold, or whether there's enough fuel to run the generator until the end of the
day," she said. "These are questions that weren't part of our job before the
war."

## **Drone Warfare**

In addition to the impact on civilians, the RSF strikes on infrastructure are
also changing the balance of the war around El-Obeid. A member of the Joint
Forces, an armed group aligned with the SAF, told Drop Site on condition of
anonymity that the military was having difficulties moving troops and supplies
as a result of RSF attacks on fuel stations and roads in the area.

The region now being contested by the two sides has become vital to the larger
war. The area under siege separates the army-controlled east of Sudan from the
RSF-controlled west. That makes it the main corridor through which the warring
parties move troops, weapons, fuel, and supplies.

For both sides, drones have become an important tool for combat, as well as a
means to punish and pressure the civilian population. In the first four months
of 2026, armed drones caused more than 80% of civilian deaths, killing at
least 880 people nationwide, with the Kordofan and Darfur regions hardest hit,
the UN [said](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/05/1167479) in May.

The drones themselves come from [outside
Sudan](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/longform/2026/2/3/drone-warfare-in-
sudan-tracking-1000-aerial-attacks-since-april-2023). According to
[international
investigations](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/longform/2026/2/3/drone-
warfare-in-sudan-tracking-1000-aerial-attacks-since-april-2023), the RSF's
fleet--including [Chinese-made](https://defence-blog.com/sudan-destroys-two-
chinese-made-ch-95-drones-in-one-operation/) CH-95 and Wing Loong II drones--
reaches the battlefield through a UAE-linked supply network routed through
Chad and Libya.

The SAF's drones, including [Iranian
Mohajer-6](https://thesudantimes.com/sudan/iran-supplying-burhans-forces-with-
drones-weapons/) and Ababil-3 models and Turkish Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci
aircraft, [reportedly
arrive](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/01/world/africa/egypt-sudan-
drones.html) with the support of Egypt, which has provided the army with
aircraft, ammunition, and military coordination throughout the war.

The current wave of attacks on El-Obeid accelerated after the historic capital
of the massive Darfur region, El-Fasher, fell in October 2025--an event that
was also followed by a [horrific
massacre](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/execution-sexual-violence-kidnapping-
el-fasher-sudan-darfur-rsf-displacement) in the city according to local
witnesses and international monitors.

On January 4, RSF drones hit El-Obeid's [city's thermal power
plant](https://sudantribune.com/article/308964?__cf_chl_tk=bYPW0Hdtkr9.nxbK.2uDvFToX7G1v.UgYhfbuKM_yE4-1784563761-1.0.1.1-JlBmMPIUoQPEvrlpR7Hs5BO.4XG5.ZF.ZM_W.VpAYIw).
The attack came as part of a wider wave that also struck the Merowe Dam and
Kenana airbase in the city. On January 30, roughly 20 RSF drones [struck
government buildings ](https://sudantribune.com/article/310055)in a rare
daytime attack.

The UN has said that drone attacks are now expanding beyond Kordofan and
Darfur into the regions of Blue Nile, White Nile, and Khartoum itself. A
strike on Khartoum International Airport [on May
4](https://sudantribune.com/article/313495) grounded all flights, raising
fears that hostilities could return to the capital after a period of relative
calm.

## **" Total Collapse of Everything"**

Civilians in El-Obeid are struggling to maintain the surviving infrastructure
in the city. A pediatrician at El-Obeid Teaching Hospital described the
situation as a "total collapse of everything," with the breakdown of supply
chains and power infrastructure depriving children of life-saving
interventions. He said he's seen numerous cases where children have died
because of the indirect impacts of airstrikes.

"The child needs blood, and we don't have any. He needs oxygen, but the
generator has stopped. He needs to be transferred to a higher-level hospital,
but no ambulance dares take the road," said the doctor, who asked to be
identified by the initials MT to protect his safety. "The drone didn't strike
this child directly. But it killed him."

The dire conditions are compounded by the rising number of displaced people
arriving from other regions as refugees. "El-Obeid is hosting growing numbers
of displaced people, while at the same time its own residents are suffering
from repeated attacks on their livelihoods, infrastructure, and basic
services," said Majdi al-Naeem of the Sudan Human Rights Monitor.

Al-Naeem said the attacks on infrastructure do not, in his view, serve any
clear military objective, but instead impose direct burdens on the civilian
population. "In my assessment, these attacks don't serve a military purpose so
much as they affect civilians' lives, and targeting civilian objects is
prohibited under international humanitarian law," he said.

On Monday, the Sudanese army and allied groups
[recaptured](https://x.com/DropSiteNews/status/2081452222693470340) Bara, Al-
Baraka, Um Sayala, Jabrat Al-Sheikh, and other areas on Sunday after heavy
clashes with the RSF, according to military officials cited by Sudan Tribune.
Officials said 73 RSF vehicles were destroyed, others seized, and numerous
fighters killed. The advance opens a new supply corridor to El-Obeid,
strengthening its eastern defenses.

For the past few weeks, talk has been spreading of a possible RSF offensive
once the city and its defenders have been sufficiently weakened by the siege.
The SAF reclaiming the highway into El-Obeid will likely disrupt the RSF's
momentum toward El-Obeid, restricting the movement of fighters, supplies, and
reinforcements.

Zahra Nurain, a mother of five living in the Karima neighborhood in the city's
northeast, said the talk of a potential large-scale battle has been a daily
source of anxiety but has not pushed her toward leaving--a reflection of the
limited choices available after more than three years of war.

"We hear the news and rumors every day, and sometimes we follow the sounds of
aircraft and explosions. But where would we go?" she said. "El-Obeid has
become a refuge for many people during this war. We hope it does not become
another battlefield."

_**Mohamed Wad Al-Sak** is a Sudanese freelance journalist and multimedia
producer covering conflict, displacement, and human rights across Sudan and
East Africa. _
